title: Air India Weighs Folding Budget Arm AI Express Into Parent Group to Trim Losses
excerpt: Incoming CEO Tewolde Gebremariam has questioned why the Tata carrier runs two separate airline companies, arguing a single group would lower regulatory costs and duplicate management.
body:
• Air India's incoming chief executive Tewolde Gebremariam is considering folding the low-cost Air India Express unit into the parent airline to cut costs, according to people familiar with the matter.
  • The CEO-designate has questioned why two airline companies need separate operating permits, arguing a single group would lower regulatory requirements and remove duplicated management, engineering and administrative staff.
  • Air India posted a loss of about ₹22,000 crore ($2.3 billion) in the year through March, adding urgency to cost-cutting at the Tata Group-owned carrier.
  • The idea is at an early stage and would require supervisory board approval; Air India Express would keep its brand name under any combination.

Air India's incoming chief executive, Tewolde Gebremariam, is weighing whether to fold the no-frills Air India Express unit into the parent airline group as he looks for ways to cut costs and reverse record losses, according to people familiar with the matter.

In meetings across departments, the former Ethiopian Airlines Group chief has quizzed managers about the need to run two airline companies with separate operating permits, the people said, asking not to be identified because the discussions were private. The deliberations show Gebremariam's eagerness to weed out inefficiencies after Air India posted a loss of ₹22,000 crore ($2.3 billion) in the year through March.

A case for one airline group

Gebremariam's argument, according to the people familiar with the discussions, is straightforward: operating a single airline group would lower regulatory requirements and reduce the need for two sets of managers, engineers and administrative staff. AI Express would keep its brand name under any combination, they said.

The idea remains at an early stage. Realising it would require approval from the supervisory board, and an Air India spokesperson did not respond to an email seeking comment, according to the report carried by The Economic Times.

The discussions land at a moment of upheaval for the airline. Gebremariam was chosen as chief executive largely because of his record of turning Ethiopian Airlines into Africa's largest and most profitable carrier during his 11 years at its helm, and his first address to staff on September 7 carried a blunt promise to "Make Air India Great Again." He is expected to formally take charge later this month as Campbell Wilson, who has led the airline since July 2022, steps down.

Losses sharpen the knife

The financial pressure is acute. Air India and Air India Express reported a combined loss of ₹22,238 crore in FY26, more than double the previous year. The June 2025 crash of flight AI171, which killed 260 people, intensified regulatory scrutiny of the carrier, and geopolitical disruptions — including the closure of Pakistani airspace to Indian carriers and Middle East conflict — have pushed fuel and operating costs higher.

Reducing losses matters beyond the airline itself. Tata Sons, which owns about 75% of Air India with Singapore Airlines holding the rest, is fighting a power struggle over chairman N. Chandrasekaran's tenure extension while facing a regulatory push to list.

What came before

Gebremariam's predecessor had already consolidated the group's structure, but from four airlines to two. Under the Vihaan.AI transformation plan, Air India absorbed Vistara and Air India Express absorbed AIX Connect (formerly AirAsia India), a merger completed in October 2024. In April 2025, Campbell Wilson stepped down as chairman of the Air India Express board, telling staff that the structural work was "largely complete" and the task at hand was to "fully leverage and optimise the group's fleet, network, sales, distribution, and loyalty assets."

AI Express, which operates more than 500 daily flights across 39 domestic and 17 international airports with a fleet of 110 aircraft, was once the profitable sibling of the group. That record has unravelled: in FY25 the low-cost arm accounted for the bulk of the group's red ink.

What's next

Any move to combine the two carriers would still need sign-off from the supervisory board, and the airline's board met in Mumbai this month to formalise Gebremariam's appointment and compensation. For now, the talks are a signal of the incoming CEO's style: an operator who ran a tightly disciplined multi-airline group in Addis Ababa, now asking why Air India needs two of them.
